connection_type: I have direct personal experience (as an immigrant, refugee, religious minority, or member of a marginalised group)
duration: I have known I was queer for 10 years and have been exploring my gender for 3
disclosure_text: Being queer has shaped my sense of self and how I interact with the world. I primarily spend time around other queer people and do not tolerate being around people with negative opinions on queerness.
micronarrative: I feel a connection with the students who describe discriminations that went unnoticed, while the posts from people who claim "reverse discrimination" anger me. This reaction stems from a sense of injustice I feel when people who have privilege see efforts to correct discrimination against minorities as attacks on them. I grew up in Maryland, where I was pretty isolated from the local culture. Moving to the south in later childhood helped me understand better, specifically between moving to a poorer and less isolated area. In this new environment, I found that people are much more social and open to talking to others. While I cannot recall a specific conversation that highlighted this shift, the contrast between my isolated upbringing and the social openness of the South shaped my understanding of community and privilege, grounding my response to the forum’s heated exchanges.

annotations.tweet_text: When a working-class white man loses a job to a diversity hire, he's not allowed to be angry. That anger has to go somewhere.
annotations.participant_label: Clearly harmful — targets a group in a way that dehumanises or incites
annotations.rationale: The comment is demeaning towards minorities by calling them "diversity hires," which implies that the skills they demonstrated to get hired aren't valid. Additionally, "That anger has to go somewhere" implies that minorities are responsible/deserving of the blame for others losing out on jobs, rather than the wider factors making the job market hostile to everyone right now, regardless of minority status.

annotations.tweet_text: Intersectionality is just a hierarchy that puts some victims above others. It's oppression with extra steps.
annotations.participant_label: Likely harmful — framing that would harm most readers from the targeted group, even if deniable
annotations.rationale: Implication that recognizing intersectionality, the concept that people belonging to multiple minority groups face worse/more oppression than people only belonging to one, is itself oppression is a harmful stance. Feeling like your experience is downplayed can be frustrating, and this comment is likely motivated by that rather than actual hate, but it leads to hate being spread.

annotations.tweet_text: First-generation immigrant women are often the most opposed to feminism. Nobody ever asks them why.
annotations.participant_label: Ambiguous — could be read as harmful or legitimate depending on who is reading and why
annotations.rationale: The comment on its' surface appears to be a neutral, even positive call to include the marginalized voices of immigrant women in discussions of feminism, but is actually intended to shut down feminist arguments. First generation immigrant women are pinnacles of intersectionality, meaning they are some of the most affected by feminist issues, so this group being "the most oppossed" to feminism should highlight a flaw in feminism. The reality is that this group is often purposefully kept uneducated and misled on these issues by their oppressors.

annotations.tweet_text: We have a word for communities where women can't leave the house without permission. We're just not allowed to use it anymore.
annotations.participant_label: Ambiguous — could be read as harmful or legitimate depending on who is reading and why
annotations.rationale: This comment is unclear in meaning when taken out of it's original context. I lean towards harmful because of the wording of the comment. The phrase "we're not allowed to say it anymore," is often used by people who want to return to "traditional values," which leads me to believe this comment might be responding to something progressive and positive in bad faith by comparing it to something oppressive. It is hard to tell without context.

reflexivity_response: While most of these responses skipped mentioning their personal identity in relation to their annotations, the few that did highlighted differences between them and I. A response I disagreed with mentioned being raised Christian. While my parents are Christian, that was a very minimal part of my upbringing, and something I do not consider myself to be. A Christian upbringing often involves using religious teachings to encourage a child to develop certain values and principles, whereas my own parents focused on teaching me certain values and principles using their real-world importance. The Christian's response falls short, in my eyes, because they take the comment (and the US justice system) at face value, whereas my analysis included factors not taken into account by the comment.
